title: Depart from me (Luke 5:1–11)
hook: after the huge catch, Peter falls down: I'm a sinful man; Jesus says fear not

segments.voice: Yesterday, a doorway at sunset, and hands laid on every one of them. Who got your full attention, phone down, to the end of their sentences? Day five hundred nineteen.

Simon has been up all night, and he has nothing to show for it: sore arms, cold hands, empty nets. He and his partners are on the shore now, washing their nets, which is the last chore before sleep. And a crowd is pressing in on a teacher by the water, so close he steps into Simon's boat and asks him to push off a little. Simon does. Jesus sits and teaches from the boat. Fine. Then, when he's finished, he turns to the tired fisherman and says something no fisherman wants to hear at the end of a bad night: let's go out again.
screen: `A NIGHT SHIFT WITH NOTHING TO SHOW.`

segments.voice: "Launch out into the deep, and let down your nets for a draught." Listen to Simon's answer in the King James words, tired and honest at once: "Master, we have toiled all the night, and have taken nothing: nevertheless at thy word I will let down the net." We have toiled. Nevertheless. That word holds both his exhaustion and his trust. And the nets fill so full they start to tear. They wave to their partners in the other boat, and both boats fill until they begin to sink. Now here's the surprise. You'd expect Simon to celebrate a catch like that. Instead: "he fell down at Jesus' knees, saying, Depart from me; for I am a sinful man, O Lord." Go away from me. In Luke's telling, Simon looks at what has just happened, then at himself, and he wants distance. People still do something like it: when kindness comes unexpectedly, some of us deflect, or joke, or say you shouldn't have. Jesus doesn't argue with Simon about whether he's a sinner. He doesn't go away either. He says: "Fear not; from henceforth thou shalt catch men." Luke's Greek word for catch here is zogreo, which lexicons give as to take alive. Not catching fish for the market, but catching to keep alive, the way you pull someone out of the water. And Luke ends: "they forsook all, and followed him." Two boats full of fish, left on the beach.
screen: `DEPART FROM ME; I AM A SINFUL MAN.`
then, large: `FEAR NOT; FROM HENCEFORTH THOU SHALT CATCH MEN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: don't hide from goodness. Settle, and breathe. Think of a time someone was kind to you and you pushed it away. A compliment you argued with. A gift you said was too much. Help you refused because you didn't want to owe anyone. Notice the small voice that says depart from me, I don't deserve this. Don't fight it; just see it. Then imagine that same kindness coming toward you again, and this time you don't step back. You let it land. Breathe in, and receive it. Breathe out, and let the old embarrassment go. If you pray, you can hear Jesus' answer to Simon as if it were spoken to you: fear not. If you don't, simply let the kindness stay. The bell holds the time.
Zogreo, Luke's Greek word for catching alive: Simon's cry after the great catch, overwhelmed by goodness, and the answer he gets instead, fear not.
Your line: fear not. The next time someone is good to you today, don't deflect. Say thank you, and let it land. Day five hundred nineteen.

howItsDone: Christians read the great catch of fish as the call of the first disciples, and some churches use "launch out into the deep" to encourage people to begin something new in faith.

fork.setup: you're Simon. the nets are tearing, the boats are sinking, and you're looking at the man who told you where to fish. what do you do?
options: haul in the fish and start counting.
fall at his knees: depart from me, I'm a sinful man.
ask him to come fishing every night.
fork.reveal: Simon falls down and asks him to go away. Jesus doesn't leave. he says: fear not.

original.note: Greek: catching alive. "thou shalt catch men": to take alive, to rescue.

trapdoor: what you thought: "depart from me" sounds like rejection.
what it means: Simon is overwhelmed by goodness and feels unworthy; Jesus answers with fear not, and stays.
what a scholar hears: before the catch Simon calls him epistata, master; after it, kyrie, Lord. the King James text keeps the shift: Master in 5:5, O Lord in 5:8.

notes: zogreo = take alive (standard lexicons). epistates as a title for Jesus appears only in Luke; Simon uses it in 5:5 and kyrie in 5:8. Confirm.
Washing nets as 'the last chore before sleep' is an illustrative picture.
'Launch out into the deep' as an encouragement phrase (e.g. Duc in altum) described generally.

Editor review (2026-10-01): cut the 'you know the feeling' hook opener, the superlatives ('one of the most honest sentences in the Gospels', 'the best catch of his life'), the claim that epistata is 'a word only Luke uses', and the generalization that people always deflect kindness; zogreo now attributed to lexicons.
